title: Air India CEO Gebremariam Gets Free Hand to Rebuild Senior Management
excerpt: Tata Sons has backed the former Ethiopian Airlines chief to hire from outside the group and restructure Air India's top team, as a Rs 22,238 crore FY26 consolidated loss sharpens the turnaround pressure.
body:
• Air India's chief executive Tewolde Gebremariam has been given a free hand by Tata Sons chairman N Chandrasekaran to rebuild the airline's senior management, including hiring executives from outside the Tata Group, according to The Economic Times reporting cited by multiple outlets.
  • Nipun Aggarwal, Air India's chief commercial and transformation officer and a central figure in the Tata takeover, could move out of executive management, with alternative roles within the group discussed.
  • Air India and Air India Express reported a consolidated net loss of Rs 22,238 crore in FY26, more than double the previous year's loss.
  • For passengers, the near-term test is operational: reliability, on-time performance and cabin upgrades — the reset itself does not change any booking, route or fare today.

Air India is preparing a senior management overhaul under its new chief executive, Tewolde Gebremariam, who has been given a free hand by Tata Sons to build his own team as the carrier tries to turn an ambitious expansion programme into a financial turnaround, people familiar with the matter told The Economic Times. Gebremariam, who led Ethiopian Airlines for more than a decade, took charge of Air India on October 1, 2026, succeeding Campbell Wilson.

According to the reporting, Tata Sons chairman N Chandrasekaran has given Gebremariam freedom to restructure the senior management, including hiring external executives with experience of running large airlines. The changes could see Nipun Aggarwal, Air India's chief commercial and transformation officer and one of the most influential members of its leadership, move out of executive management. Chandrasekaran and Aggarwal have discussed the possibility, with the Tata Sons chairman understood to have offered him alternative roles within the group, the report said. Air India did not comment.

The financial backdrop

The reset comes as the carrier faces mounting pressure to improve performance. Air India and Air India Express reported a consolidated net loss of Rs 22,238 crore for the year ended March 2026, more than double the Rs 10,859 crore loss a year earlier, according to the Economic Times figures reported by Live From A Lounge. Consolidated expenses rose to Rs 93,733 crore in FY26 from Rs 89,317 crore in the previous year, as revenue declined.

Gebremariam has been candid about the core problem. Speaking at the Aviation India and South Asia conference in November, he acknowledged that Air India's cost per available seat kilometre is higher than its revenue per available seat kilometre — in plain terms, the airline spends more operating its capacity than it earns from it. Shortly after he took charge, the airline set up a cross-functional team to identify savings across the organisation, tightened spending approvals and introduced an initiative encouraging employees to suggest ways to reduce costs or increase revenue.

Integration and network plans

Separately, Reuters reported that Air India and Air India Express are set to integrate their operations more closely to address cost and operational challenges, while retaining separate Air Operator Certificates, and that the airline is set to create a new Group Strategy Officer role as part of the changes. The closer integration with the low-cost unit is part of the wider restructuring under consideration.

On the network side, Gebremariam is reassessing Air India's hub structure. The airline has historically concentrated much of its international operation around Delhi, with Mumbai as another key gateway; the new plan looks at strengthening Mumbai's role in international operations, including additional services to Europe and North America, with Bengaluru identified as a potential third hub. He has also indicated that Air India would like to increase its widebody aircraft orders, and the airline is exploring converting 13 older Boeing 777s into cargo freighters.

What it means for passengers

Nothing in the reported overhaul changes a ticket, a route or a fare today. For the diaspora reader who flies Air India between India and North America, Europe or the Gulf, the measures that matter will be the operational ones Gebremariam is expected to set out — reliability, on-time performance and the pace of cabin refurbishment. A company-wide town hall was scheduled for Wednesday afternoon, at which he was expected to roll out the next set of changes. Whether the leadership reset delivers them will be judged on the operation, not the org chart.
